deep.reconstruction:
OVERVIEW. The page converts parabolic comet elements into 'Gaussian constants' for heliocentric equatorial coordinates (Theoria Motus, art. 53-58 style). It then evaluates one geocentric position.

Symbols: n = longitude of node Omega, i = inclination, eps = obliquity, omega = argument of perihelion, v = true anomaly, u = v + omega.

Identification (mine). The elements are i ~ 63deg12', Omega ~ 266deg38', omega = 4deg21'42.12'', and log q = 9.8114927 (q = 0.64766). These match the Great Comet of 1807 (C/1807 R1), which Gauss computed.

Input logs, all checked:
- log cos i = 9.6539100, log sin i = 9.9506879, log tan i = 0.2967779.
- log tan n = 1.2315447, log cos n = 8.7677091n, log sin n = 9.9992537n. So n is in the third quadrant, about 266.6deg.

1. x-COORDINATE (unchanged by rotating ecliptic to equator).
- Unit vectors in the orbit plane give x = r sin a sin(A+u).
- Defining equations: sin a sin A = cos Omega and sin a cos A = -sin Omega cos i.
- Hence cot A = -cos i tan Omega: 9.6539100 + 1.2315447 = 0.8854547n. This gives A = 352deg34'58.54''.
- log sin A = 9.1108962n.
- sin a = cos Omega / sin A: 8.7677091 - 9.1108962 = 9.6568129.
- cos a = sin i sin Omega: 9.9506879 + 9.9992537 = 9.9499416, negative. This is the x direction cosine of the orbit pole.

2. AUXILIARY ANGLES E AND F.
- tan E = tan i / cos Omega: 0.2967779 - 8.7677091 = 1.5290688n, so E = 91deg41'38.59''. E is the direction in the y-z plane of the u = 90deg vector (cos Omega cos i, sin i).
- tan F = tan i cos Omega: 0.2967779 + 8.7677091 = 9.0644870n, so F = 173deg22'58.17''. F is the direction of the orbit plane's trace in the y-z plane.
- Obliquity, written as '327 48 70': eps = 23deg27'48.70''.
- Hence eps+E = 115deg9'27.29'' and eps+F = 196deg50'46.87''.

3. y- AND z-CONSTANTS. With g = cos Omega cos i / cos E:
- y' = r[cos u sin Omega cos eps + sin u g cos(eps+E)].
- z' = r[cos u sin Omega sin eps + sin u g sin(eps+E)].
- Hence cot B = cos i cot Omega cos(eps+E) / (cos E cos eps).
- And cot C = cos i cot Omega sin(eps+E) / (cos E sin eps).
- Common factor: log cos i cot n = 8.4223653; minus log cos E 8.4707413n gives 9.9516240n.
- Column B: + compl. log cos eps 0.0374821 + log cos(eps+E) 9.6285006n = 9.6176067. So B = 247deg28'55.77'' (a first entry 247deg8'55.32'' is struck out).
- Column C: + compl. log sin eps 0.3999367 + log sin(eps+E) 9.9567167 = 0.3082774n. So C = 333deg48'55.74''.
- sin b = sin Omega cos eps / sin B: 9.9625179 + 9.9992537 + 0.0344407 = 9.9962123.
- sin c = sin Omega sin eps / sin C: 9.6000633 + 9.9992537 + 0.3553021 = 9.9546191.

4. CHECK VIA POLE DIRECTION COSINES.
- log(cos i / cos F) = 9.6539100 - 9.9970972n = 9.6568128n. This equals log sin a, an identity since cos^2 i + sin^2 i cos^2 Omega = 1 - cos^2 a.
- Adding log sin(eps+F) 9.4621076n gives 9.1189204n = log cos b. Thus b = 97deg33'22.27''.
- Adding log cos(eps+F) 9.9809507n gives 9.6377635 = log cos c. Thus c = 64deg15'39.28''; c is also the equatorial inclination.
- These agree with sin b and sin c from step 3. Struck trial values 93deg23', 93deg31', 98deg12' precede b.

5. FINAL CONSTANTS FOR TRUE ANOMALY. In the parabola r = q sec^2(v/2), so x = q sec^2(v/2) sin a sin(v + A + omega), and likewise for y, z.
- Right margin: 9.8114927 (log q) together with log sin a, sin b, sin c.
- log q + log sin a, b, c = 9.4683056, 9.8077050, 9.7661118.
- A+omega = 356deg56'40.66'', B+omega = 251deg50'37.89'', C+omega = 338deg10'37.86''.
- The common differences give omega = 4deg21'42.12'' exactly.

6. ONE EPHEMERIS POINT (v ~ 68.2deg, 5-place logs). log r = 9.9754, sec^2(v/2) = 1.459.
- x = r sin a sin(v+A') from 9.63219 + 9.95779, giving +0.38903.
- y = r sin b sin(v+B') from 9.97159 + 9.80766n, giving -0.60151.
- z = r sin c sin(v+C') from 9.93000 + 9.85969, giving +0.61616.
- Sun's equatorial coordinates (X, Y, Z) = (-0.87436, -0.43436, -0.18853). Here Z/Y = tan eps, the Sun's distance is 0.994 and its longitude is about 208deg (late October 1807).
- Geocentric sums: -0.48533, -1.03587, +0.42763.
- log y 0.01531, log x 9.68604, so alpha = 244deg53'45''. A struck first value is 261deg41'57''.
- log sin alpha 9.95691, giving log(rho cos delta) = 0.05840.
- log z 9.63107, so tan delta gives delta = 20deg29'49''.
- log cos delta 9.97160, so log rho = 0.08680 (rho = 1.221).
- The block 9.99754, 9.94445n, 9.96006, 9.67779n, 9.59760 and the numbers 6973348, 6031274 are not securely identified.

7. MARGINALIA (unrelated). Theta-series jottings:
- (1-2x+2x^4-...)/(1+2x+2x^4+...), i.e. theta4/theta3.
- 2x+2x^3+2x^9+2x^27 (reading uncertain).
- An infinite product (1-x)(1-x^3)(1-x^9)...
- A coefficient table for exponents 0..15 and a polynomial, both written mirror-wise. These are likely coefficient counts of a product expansion, continuing on the next page's product manipulations.
errors: The line 'a 116.59.3.42' does not fit the stated sin a = 0.45374 (log 9.6568129) and cos a = -0.89112 (log 9.9499416n). These give a = 153deg0'56.58''; 116deg59'3.42'' differs from 26deg59'3.42'' (the reference angle) by exactly 90deg. Either the transcription/reading is wrong or Gauss wrote a slip, possibly a quadrant/label issue. The angle a is not used later; only sin a is used, so nothing downstream is affected.
B was first entered as 247deg8'55.32'' and corrected to 247deg28'55.77''. The corrected value checks: cot B = 0.414579 gives 67deg28'55.8'' + 180deg.

Column labels are loose but the numbers are consistent. 'cos eps' denotes the arithmetic complement of log cos eps. In the second column the entry under 'cos eps+E' is log sin(eps+E), and the entry under 'cos eps' is the complement of log sin eps.
Otherwise every log addition/subtraction checked agrees to within 1 unit of the 7th decimal.

results.what: Reduction of orbital elements (Omega, i, omega, eps) to constants a, A, b, B, c, C with x = r sin a sin(A+u) etc., using auxiliary angle E (tan E = tan i / cos Omega) to rotate from ecliptic to equator
results.modern_name: Gaussian vectorial constants / P,Q orientation vectors (equatorial)

results.what: Check via direction cosines of the orbit pole: cos a = sin i sin Omega, cos b = -cos i sin(eps+F)/cos F, cos c = cos i cos(eps+F)/cos F (equatorial inclination), with tan F = tan i cos Omega; also |cos i / cos F| = sin a
results.modern_name: Orbit-normal vector components / transformation of inclination and node to the equator

results.what: Ephemeris point: heliocentric equatorial coordinates of the parabolic comet plus solar coordinates, giving geocentric RA 244deg53'45'', Dec 20deg29'49'', log distance 0.08680
Marginal theta-series ratio (1-2x+2x^4-...)/(1+2x+2x^4+...) and infinite products (1-x)(1-x^3)(1-x^9)..., coefficient tables
results.modern_name: Jacobi theta functions theta3, theta4; q-series product expansions
results.usually_credited_to: Jacobi (1829) for the published theory; Gauss's unpublished work c. 1800 is documented in Werke III/X

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a routine working sheet applying Gauss's own published method for comet coordinate constants, apparently for the Great Comet of 1807, plus one ephemeris position. The theta-series marginalia match Gauss's well-documented unpublished q-series interests and are too fragmentary to establish anything new.

checkable.asserts: log|cot A| = log cos i + log tan Omega
log tan E = log tan i - log|cos Omega|
log tan F = log tan i + log|cos Omega|
log sin eps = 9.6000633, so its complement is 0.3999367, not 0.3994367
same omega = 4deg21'42.12'' added to A and B (result 0)
cos^2 a + cos^2 b + cos^2 c = 1 (approx 0.9999)
(cos i / cos F)^2 = sin^2 a when tan F = tan i cos Omega (result 0)
solar coordinates satisfy Z = Y tan eps (Sun on ecliptic)

transcription_corrections: 'cos eps ... 0,3994367' should read 0,3999367; it is the complement of log sin eps = 9.6000633.
'327 48 70' is the obliquity 23deg27'48.70'', written above E.
In the second column, the entry under 'cos eps+E' is log sin(eps+E) = 9.9567167.
'sin v + 356.56.40,66' etc. means sin(v + 356deg56'40.66''); these are the constants A+omega, B+omega, C+omega.
The bottom table numbers and polynomial are written mirror-reversed: the index row is 15 14 ... 1 0.
